steps.title: Five platform parameters
notes: Laser timing is a platform group (FLAGS.PLATFORM): it describes the scanner of the machine, not the part. ATU reads it from the profile that is set as the platform profile.

Jump speed is the speed of the spot while the laser is off. The delays are waiting times of the mirrors, in microseconds. Minimum jump delay and jump length limit make short jumps wait less; the limit 0 (default) switches that off.

lines: // Used for the power optimization, the exposure time estimate and the
// LSR time column. jump_speed (mm/s): speed of the laser spot while the
// laser is off. mark_delay / jump_delay (microseconds): waiting times of
// the scanner after a marked sequence (every hatch vector, once per
// contour) / after a jump, so the mirrors can settle before the next
// action. min_jump_delay / jump_length_limit: jumps shorter than the
// limit get a delay between min_jump_delay (length 0) and jump_delay
// so every jump gets the full jump delay.

steps.title: Read and check
notes: read_platform_settings keeps the delays in microseconds (_us); every user converts them itself. The time calculations divide by the jump speed, so the validation rejects a jump speed of 0, and with the scaling switched on a minimum jump delay above the full jump delay.

lines: // The time calculations divide by the jump speed.
r_errors.push('Laser timing: jump speed must be greater than 0');
// A minimum above the full delay would make short jumps slower than
// long ones; only checked when the scaling is switched on.
r_errors.push('Laser timing: minimum jump delay must not be greater than the jump delay');

steps.title: Short jumps, short delay
notes: A short jump moves the mirrors only a little, so they settle faster. scaled_jump_delay gives jumps shorter than the limit a delay on a straight line from the minimum (length 0) to the full jump delay (length = limit). Longer jumps get the full delay.

Missing or invalid settings give the full delay, and a jump of (almost) zero length gets none. The time estimate, the power optimization, the laser assignment and the LSR time column all call this one function, so they cannot disagree.

lines: // The negated comparisons are also true for undefined and NaN, so
// missing or invalid scaling settings give the full delay.

steps.title: The time of one path
notes: add_path_time adds, for one path: the jump from the last laser position with its jump delay, the marking (length ÷ speed of the vector type), the jumps between the vectors of a hatch block with their delays, and the mark delays.

A mark delay is spent every time the laser switches off: after every hatch vector, but only once at the end of a contour, whose corners are marked without stopping. On the hatch plate a layer has 471 hatch vectors and one border: 472 mark delays.

lines: function add_path_time(a_laser, a_path, a_first, a_last, a_speed, a_timing_ms)
let l_jump = MATH.dist(a_laser.pos.x, a_laser.pos.y, a_first.x, a_first.y);
// getExposureLength: total length with laser on (mm).
// getSkipLength / getSkipCount: total length and number of the
// jumps between the vectors of a hatch (0 for contours and open
// polylines, which are marked without interruption).
// Only the total skip length is known, not every single jump, so
// the delay is taken for the mean jump length. This is exact while
// all jumps are shorter than the length limit (the delay is linear
// there) or the scaling is off; otherwise it is a slight
// overestimate. Reading every jump would cost far more time.
// A closed contour ends where it started.

steps.title: One clock per laser
notes: estimate_layer_time_ms walks through the paths in their final exposure order. Each path counts for the laser in its laser_index attribute: every laser has its own clock and its own last position, because the lasers work at the same time.
The layer is finished when the slowest laser is finished, so the result is the maximum, not the sum. With a single laser every path counts for laser 0.

steps.title: From the layers to the build
notes: The layer times are calculated in parallel, after the sorting, the laser assignment and the power optimization, and stored as tray attributes, one per layer. A single-threaded step adds them up into built_time_estimation_ms, the attribute the host reads.
The export writes the total into export_info.json as estimated_exposure_time_ms. Recoating and acceleration are not included: it is the time the lasers need, not the build time of the machine.

steps.title: The same rules in the power optimization
notes: The power optimization converts its two vector lengths into return times with reference_time_ms: marking, mark delay, the jump of one hatch distance and its jump delay, scaled like every other jump. For a 0.5 mm vector that is 0.42 ms of marking and 0.07 ms of delays and jump.
Both reference times contain the same delays, and the return time of a vector contains them as well: the delays move both ends of the power range together with the vectors.

lines: // length / speed gives seconds; * 1000 -> ms. Delays: us / 1000 -> ms.

steps.title: The time column of the LSR export
notes: The LSR writer keeps its own clock: every real jump adds jump time and the scaled jump delay, every edge its marking time. The mark delay follows every hatch line and the last edge of a polyline. The start time of each vector is written as the last column of the file.

lines: let l_jump = MATH.dist(a_state.pos.x, a_state.pos.y, a_x, a_y);
// Values that are the same for every line of the record are formatted once.
// The start time of this vector includes the jump to its start point.
a_state.t_s += MATH.dist(l_x0, l_y0, l_x1, l_y1) / l_speed;
// A hatch line is a vector of its own; a polyline is one vector.

recipes.title: The timing of your scanner
recipes.why: The defaults are typical values. With the delays of your machine the estimate gets closer to the real exposure time.
recipes.result: New profiles start with a mark delay of 120 µs. Set the new profile as platform profile, rebuild and export: export_info.json holds the new estimate.

recipes.title: Shorter delays for short jumps
recipes.why: Your scanner controller scales the jump delay with the jump length, typically below about 1 mm.
recipes.result: The 0.1 mm jumps between hatch lines wait 14 µs instead of 50 µs. On the hatch plate that saves 468 × 36 µs ≈ 17 ms per layer, about 1.7 s for 100 layers; try it in the Jump delay view of the explainer.

recipes.title: A slower jump speed
recipes.why: Machines with heavy mirrors jump slower; on parts with many islands the jumps then add up.
recipes.result: New profiles assume 3000 mm/s for jumps. Try it in the explainer: on the hatch plate the jumps are only 0.1 mm long, so the estimate barely changes.

recipes.title: No jump delay for hatch jumps
recipes.why: Some scanners skip the settling time on the short jump to the next hatch line. The estimate then only counts the delay of real jumps between paths.
recipes.result: The estimate drops by one jump delay per jump inside a hatch block. The explainer's model of the hatch plate gives 468 × 50 µs ≈ 23 ms per layer, about 2.3 s for 100 layers.

edits.after: // no jump delay for the short jumps between the vectors of a hatch block
